name: Vulcan-Spit
geological_features: Surface almost entirely covered by active lava flows and caldera systems
Tidal flexing from its parent gas giant drives continuous volcanic eruption cycles
Sulfur dioxide plume columns reaching 60 kilometers above the surface
specific_features: A lava lake occupying a 90-kilometer caldera that has been continuously active for recorded history
Periodic eruptions that launch molten material into escape velocity, creating a faint debris ring
Surface color shifts between black, red, and sulphurous yellow depending on eruption state
resources: Rare earth elements concentrated in volcanic ejecta
Geothermal energy potential if harnessed from orbit
description: Vulcan-Spit is less a world than a wound, a moon-sized volcanic body locked in tortured orbit around a gas giant whose gravitational kneading keeps its interior in a state of perpetual molten agony. The surface is a shifting mosaic of black basalt crust, glowing lava rivers, and open calderas that belch sulfur dioxide into a choking toxic atmosphere. At 780 kilometers in diameter it barely qualifies as a planetary body, but what it lacks in size it compensates for in sheer violent energy output.

The atmosphere is a dense yellow-brown miasma of sulfur compounds and volcanic particulates, opaque enough to obscure the surface from orbit during peak eruption cycles. When the plumes thin, the view from above is hellish and mesmerizing: rivers of incandescent orange tracing fracture patterns across a charcoal landscape, punctuated by the white-hot eyes of active vents. The heat output is so intense that nearby vessels must maintain significant standoff distance or risk thermal damage to hull plating.

Early prospectors identified Vulcan-Spit as a source of rare earth elements concentrated by volcanic processes into unusually pure deposits. Three robotic extraction attempts were made, and three robotic extractors were consumed by lava flows within weeks of deployment. The moon's surface is simply too dynamic for any fixed installation; the crust recycles itself on timescales measured in days rather than millennia. The debris ring created by material launched into orbit by the most violent eruptions contains the same valuable elements, leading to proposals for ring-mining as an alternative.

Vulcan-Spit serves primarily as a navigational hazard and a spectacle. Pilots give it wide berth due to the unpredictable ejecta trajectories, and the sulfur plumes can foul sensor arrays at surprising distances. For those willing to risk the approach, however, it offers one of the most visually dramatic sights in charted space: a tiny world tearing itself apart and rebuilding in real time, an engine of geological creation and destruction operating at a pace that makes planetary processes feel almost biological.
